20350-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-14-no-:
The Atlantic Monthly for September 1864, volume fourteen, number eighty-three, appeared mid-Civil War. One essay warns of a gradual, general increase of insanity in the land. Statistics reveal that rise, it says, to any who care to look. A provident people should weigh what unchecked growth might bring.

If sanity is a glory all might lose unawares, the essay asks. Then all should ask if they are in their wits at this moment. Such grave pieces sat beside poems and tales in the Monthly. Readers get a stark window on wartime America's anxious mind.
21009-the-atlantic-monthly-volume-17-no-:
A born Londoner of part Italian stock defines his ground in The Atlantic Monthly for February 1866. A government clerk by trade, he writes with a traveller's roving eye besides. Volume seventeen, number one hundred opens with his frank self-portrait.

The Atlantic Monthly set America's literary tone from its Boston home. Essays, tales, poems, and reviews of high polish fill each monthly number. This February issue came as the nation healed from civil war. Its pages show the magazine at work, binding a bruised republic back together with letters, thought, and art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baldassare-pe:
Baldassare Peruzzi was an architect and painter born at Siena in 1481, who died at Rome in 1537. He apprenticed under Bramante, Raphael, and Sangallo during the building of St Peter's. His Palazzo Massimi alle Colonne, begun in 1535, shows his independent genius. Critics also ascribe the Villa Farnesina to him, with wings off a central hall and a fine exterior frieze.

Most of the villa's interior paintings are his, though its façade decoration has nearly perished. On a vault he painted the firmament with zodiac, planets, and stars, in perspective that deceived even Titian. In the Vatican's Stanza d'Eliodoro, Raphael designed the murals, but the ceiling's tapestry-like frescoes are Peruzzi's. Later works, such as the Madonna with Saints in Rome and the Augustus and Sibyl at Siena, show his growth. He also shaped decorative art widely, furnishing designs for craftsmen of many kinds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-gozzi:
Carlo Gozzi was a Venetian author born in 1720 who died in 1806. After three years of military service and with family means wasted, he turned with his brother Gasparo to literature. Joining the conservative Accademia dei Granelleschi, he attacked the two leading playwrights of the day. Chiari drew fire for ignorance and bombast, and Goldoni for a reform that would abolish the native commedia dell'arte.

To show a popular Venetian form, he wrote his Fiabe, improbable tales drawn from Basile's Cunto de li cunti and the French Cabinet des fées. Oriental collections and Spanish plays fed them too, shaped by his own fancy and sharp satire. Little order or rule governs the Fiabe, yet they made his name. His Memorie, translated by Symonds in 1890, and a Venice edition of his works in 1802 close the entry's account.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christopher-m:
An entry on Christopher Madruzzi, Prince-Bishop of Trent and cardinal, born of a noble Trent family in July 1512. He studied at Padua and Bologna, gained a Trent canonry and the parish of Tirol in 1529. He became canon of Salzburg in 1536 and of Brixen in 1537, and Prince-Bishop of Trent in 1539. Still only a subdeacon, he rose through deacon, priest, and bishop in 1542, and Paul the Third made him cardinal in 1543.

Madruzzi served Charles the Fifth and Ferdinand as a trusted envoy in delicate missions and championed the Church against Luther at the Diet of Ratisbon in 1541. As cardinal, bishop, and temporal ruler of Trent, he played a leading part at the Council of Trent. He pressed that church reform be taken up in earnest alongside doctrine in every session, in hopes of winning Protestants back. He resigned Trent in 1567 and died at Tivoli in July 1578.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cola-di-rienz:
Umberto Benigni's entry follows Cola di Rienzi, Nicola son of Lorenzo. He was a Roman tribune, a striking figure of his age. His father kept an inn near the Trastevere. Rumor made Cola a son of Emperor Henry VII. Raised at Anagni after his mother's death, he learned Latin. He steeped himself in Livy, Cicero, and Seneca. Then he worked as a notary in a Rome torn by noble factions, while the popes sat at Avignon.

His brother's death in a brawl between the Orsini and the Colonna fixed his aim. He would break the barons and restore Rome's old justice and splendor. Sent to Avignon in 1343, he begged Clement VI to return and grant the jubilee. Later he dreamed of a restored Roman Empire under an Italian emperor. He escaped his enemies once. In the end a crowd rose and slew him, dragging his body through the streets.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-bar:
Francesco Bartolozzi, born at Florence in 1727 and dead at Lisbon in 1815, was an engraver, etcher, and painter whose stipple work set a new standard for grace in print. His father, a goldsmith, taught him the burin, and by ten he had engraved two heads that promised his future powers. After study in the Florentine Academy and an apprenticeship to the Venetian engraver Wagner, he went to Rome, then to Venice, where his fame grew fast.

In 1764 Dalton, librarian to King George III, brought him to England, where he became Engraver to the King and a Royal Academician. In London he engraved more than two thousand plates, nearly all in stipple or red-chalk style. They were devoted to the human figure in sweet, tender types of beauty, with delicate light and shade and a roundness suggesting flesh never before seen in engraving. Though a reproductive artist, his drawing was superb.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-mel:
Francesco Melzi, born at Milan about 1490 and dead in 1568, was a Milanese nobleman remembered as the friend and heir of Leonardo da Vinci. Vasari calls him exceedingly handsome and says he owned the principal part of Leonardo's anatomical drawings. On Leonardo's death he inherited the master's manuscripts, instruments, books, and drawings, and gave both Vasari and Lomazzo notes on Leonardo's life. To Melzi we owe the preservation of that wonderful collection of writings.

Whether Melzi was a painter himself remains uncertain. No authentic work by him can be named, Vasari says nothing of artistic talent, and a 1523 letter hints only that he painted as an amateur. Some writers have exalted him into Leonardo's favourite and best pupil, attributing to him pictures at Berlin, Bergamo, Vaprio, and Isola Bella, but all without definite authority. The entry leaves him as Il Conte, a mysterious figure at the edge of Leonardo's legend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-xavie:
Francis Xavier Patrizi, born at Rome on 19 June 1797 and dead there on 23 April 1881, was a Jesuit exegete, a scholar who explains Scripture. Eldest son and heir of Count Patrizi, he entered the Society of Jesus in 1814 and was ordained in 1824. He soon became professor of Sacred Scripture and Hebrew at the Roman College. The revolution of 1848 drove him and his colleague Perrone to England, where he taught Jesuit scholastics, and later at Louvain. Peace restored him to Rome, where the revolution of 1870 ended his teaching career.

He wrote twenty-one biblical and ascetical works, including studies on interpreting Scripture, on the agreement of the two books of Maccabees, on the Gospels in three volumes. His commentaries on John, Mark, and Acts, a hundred psalms translated literally from Hebrew with commentary. Works on the Immaculate Conception and on Paul's words in whom all have sinned complete the list.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-martin:
George Martinuzzi, a monk, bishop, and cardinal born in Dalmatia in 1482, steered Hungary between Habsburg and Turk. Born Utjesenovic, he took his mother's name Martinuzzi, served Duke John Corvinus's court from eight, and entered the Pauline monastery near Ofen in 1504. As prior he won John Zapolya's trust, becoming royal counselor and treasurer in 1529 and bishop of Grosswardein in 1534, though papal approval waited five years.

On Zapolya's death in 1540 Martinuzzi guarded the infant John Sigismund with Petrovich, proclaimed him king, and won the sultan's recognition against Ferdinand's claim. He organized armies, raised funds, and advised Queen Isabella through the wars that followed. Ferdinand's general Castaldo at last had him murdered on the night of December 16, 1551. Julius III excommunicated the killers, lifting the sentence in 1555.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-anto:
Giovanni Antonio Cavazzi of Montecuccolo was a Capuchin friar of Bologna province, whose birth date is uncertain, who died at Genoa in 1692. In 1654 he sailed with a band of friars to the Congo, to replace brothers dead or broken by sickness. He suffered much on the long sea voyage, yet landed with zeal unabated. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows his many years of labor there.

Invalided home, he was called by the Propaganda to report on the mission, and the summons gave him the idea of writing down what he had seen. He finished a large work, but was sent back to the mission almost at once. Superiors gave the manuscript to Fortunato da Bologna, who rewrote it in finer style and published it at Bologna in 1687 as a description of Congo, Matamba, and Angola.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-cozz:
Giuseppe Cozza-Luzi was an Italian savant and Abbot of the Basilian monastery of Grottaferrata near Rome, born at Bolsena on 24 December 1837, who died there on 1 June 1905. He entered the monastery young and became abbot in 1882, winning the regard of Pius IX and later Leo XIII. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scholar of manuscripts, art, and archaeology.

Freed from official cares in 1898, he gave himself to study and won distinction by editions of ancient Vatican manuscripts. Under his direction came the phototype edition of the Codex Vaticanus in five volumes of 1889. With Carlo Vercellone he supervised the printing of its Greek text from 1868 to 1881. His most important scientific work published fragments of Strabo's Geography in 1884, first found by Cardinal Mai, who missed their importance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-lanzi: A 1913 entry on Lanzi — the Jesuit art historian. Gerhard Gietmann honors his famous Storia. His pen ordered the Italian schools. The galleries prized the weighty tome. The eighteenth century knew his name. His 1810 death is famed. His 1792 Storia is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luigi-mozzi: A 1913 entry on Mozzi — the Jesuit writer. Andrew MacErlean catalogs his works. Little is known of his career. The eighteenth century was his era. The order prized its learned son. His 1790 works are famed. His 1790 writings are famed. His 1790 Jesuit pages are famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-migazzi: A 1913 entry on Migazzi — the Vienna cardinal. Cölestin Wolfsgrüber notes his famous see. Few details of his life remain. The eighteenth century was his age. Austria knew his name. His 1803 death is famed. His 1757 Vienna is famed. His 1757 imperial see is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piazzi: Giuseppe Piazzi was the monk-astronomer who discovered the asteroid Ceres in 1801. This entry covers his career, his observatory at Palermo, and his fame. The priest who found a new world: his tiny Ceres opened the vast asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pietro-pompon: Pomponazzi was the Paduan philosopher who denied the soul's immortality could be proved by reason. This entry covers his career, his doctrines, and his condemnation. The scandal of the Renaissance schools: his daring De Immortalitate shocked learned Padua to its core.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-mary-ma: St. Mary Magdalen de' Pazzi was the Carmelite mystic of Florence. This entry examines her ecstasies, her counsels, and her fame. The bride of the Florentine cloister: her rapt ecstasies moved the city of Florence in the 1580s' convent of the Carmelites.
podcast-dannyjones-YnDW4ythQZI:
Former LSD kingpin Seth Ferranti shares his secrets with Danny Jones in this episode. Ferranti ran a major acid distribution network as a young man, then served a long federal prison sentence. He came out a writer, telling the story of the acid empire's rise and fall.

Ferranti describes how the LSD trade worked at its peak, from chemists to street dealers. He covers the manhunt, the trial, and the decades behind bars that followed. Jones asks what that life cost him and what he learned. Curious listeners get a wild life told straight by the man who lived it.
podcast-joerogan-xEBeQH39CZI:
Fighter Aljamain Sterling headlines Rogan's MMA Show number 184. Sterling held a top title with a grappling-heavy style. His wrestling base made him a hard puzzle for rivals.

Rogan breaks down Sterling's fights and ground game in detail. They talk about cuts, camps, and the cost of each camp. Sterling explains how he studies rivals on tape. The episode suits fight fans who love the chess side of the sport: grips, scrambles, and the small choices that decide who leaves with a belt. His calm in talk contrasts with his cage pressure.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-02-no-11-sep:
Eloquence opens the September 1858 Atlantic. Music masters teach that whoever can speak can sing, the essay begins; so, too, every man is eloquent once in his life. Men differ only in the heat at which they boil.

One man catches fire in parlor talk, with a shallow two-inch zeal. Another needs a crowd and a public debate, a third an opponent or hot anger, a fourth a revolution. A fifth needs nothing less than the grandeur of pure ideas, heaven and hell themselves. A crowd, the essay adds, catches the flame from one speaker and turns hearers into conductors of the charge.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-04-no-23-sep:
The life and works of Ary Scheffer lead the September 1859 Atlantic. No painter of the age, the writer claims, has pressed so deep on the popular mind of America. Few living artists are so at home at American firesides, known and loved in the remotest towns.

Few of Scheffer's own canvases have been shown in the country, yet engravings from them are familiar to every person of taste. Young maidens love their tender sadness, the essay says, and suffering hearts find comfort in their pure, high faith. Such an effect must have a cause, and the writer finds it in the aim and character of the artist himself, whose two leading traits the piece goes on to name.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-06-no-35-sep:
Among the Trees leads the September 1860 Atlantic. Whoever studies trees, the essay begins, must be struck by their worth, not only for the beauty of a landscape but for the whole economy of life. In no other part of the plant world has Nature done so much for the comfort, food, and shelter of her creatures.

Trees house wild animals and feed them in large part. Man in a state of nature weaves his tent from their branches and thatches it with their leaves. He hunts in their shades for flesh and furs, and takes from their wood the tools to catch his prey. His earliest meal-food, too, came from trees.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-08-no-47-sep:
The Shakespeare Mystery leads the September 1861 Atlantic. In 1853, the essay recalls, a joyful cry rose at the printing of Mr. Collier's Notes and Emendations to the text of Shakespeare's plays, drawn from early manuscript corrections. Doubt and strife, it was said, were at an end.

The shout had hardly died before a counter cry of warning rose from a few firm lips. Growing mouth by mouth, it drowned the first. The fight over the margin readings in that famed volume has now ended. Nearly all the readings peculiar to it have been rejected. The verdict also goes against any show of authority in them at all.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-10-no-59-sep:
David Gaunt, a story, leads the September 1862 Atlantic under a German motto from Goethe's Faust about the spirit of the times. It opens by asking what sort of sword old Christian carried in his famous fight with Apollyon, long ago. He cut the fiend to the marrow at last, the writer recalls, though the battle went hard with him for a time.

Some of Christian's blood, Bunyan says, is on the stones of that valley to this day. The strange little valley fades back from the sober freshness of a summer morning: its lasting twilight, lily-crusted meadows, and herd-boy's quiet song, close upon the borders of hell. Then the view shifts to busy early streets, children racing to school, and willows shimmering in sunlight.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-12-no-71-sep:
The Puritan Minister leads the September 1863 Atlantic. The hour is nine on a summer Sabbath morning, in a year of the sixteen hundreds. Sunlight falls on a small forest settlement. Around its growing fields the great American wilderness draws back day by day.

Bears, wolves, and Indians withdraw ever farther off. Yet the stout wooden gates closing the village street at both ends keep their meaning. The place would look busy and thriving today but for the Sabbath stillness brooding over it in almost excess of calm. Smoke rises more faintly than usual. Since three o'clock the day before, worldly work has wholly stopped.
the-atlantic-monthly-volume-18-no-110-de:
December 1866 leads with John Pierpont. Most men of fourscore and upward, the essay says, who have been mightily abused in their day are found on close inquiry to have long outlived themselves. Here is a man who, in his eighty-second year, kept his edge to the very last.

He held the temper of a Damascus blade, the writer says. Its bright blue rippling glitter stayed with him. Or rather, he held the temper of that strange tool found among the ruins of Thebes. That tool was once used to smooth and polish. The piece sums up a long, fighting life at its close, measuring how a poet and reformer stayed sharp when age dulls most men.
